---
title: "Data format"
description: "One CSV plus one YAML sidecar, for every acquisition"
toc: true
toc-depth: 4
---

Every AMLab acquisition — a single reading repeated a thousand times, a three
second stream, a day of temperature logging — is stored the same way: **one
CSV file with the samples, and one YAML file with the same stem carrying
everything you would otherwise have to remember**.

```
experiments/S1-daq-static/data/
├── reference.csv     # t_us,pin,raw
└── reference.yaml    # who, what, which board, which host, how it went
```

The reason for the split is that the CSV must stay trivially readable by
anything — `pandas`, `readr`, a spreadsheet, `awk` — while the metadata needs
structure. The reason for insisting on the sidecar at all is that half the
experiments on this site treat the acquisition conditions as *influence
quantities*: the host operating system, the board's reference voltage, the
requested versus achieved sampling rate. A CSV without its sidecar is not a
measurement, it is a column of numbers.

## The CSV {#sec-csv}

Long format, exactly as produced by `arduino-io stream --csv`:

```{.default filename="reference.csv"}
t_us,pin,raw
1043216,15,8103
1043216,16,19821
1044216,15,8110
1044216,16,19825
```

- **`t_us`** — the *device's* `micros()` value for the record, as an integer.
  Not host arrival time. Samples belonging to the same record share a
  timestamp, because the board reads its selected channels in one pass of
  `loop()`.
- **`pin`** — the Arduino pin number, as an integer. Which physical input that
  is depends on the board: A0 is pin 15 on a Portenta H7 and pin 14 on an UNO
  R4, so the pin-to-quantity mapping lives in the sidecar's `channels` block
  and nowhere else.
- **`raw`** or **`volts`** — the sample. `raw` is the ADC code as the board
  reported it; `volts` is that code converted by the driver. Exactly one of
  the two must be present.

::: {.callout-important}
## Raw files get exactly these three columns

Derived columns — a calibrated temperature, a filtered signal, a residual —
belong in a *processed* file, written next to the raw one with a different
stem (`run03-processed.csv`). A raw file is what came off the board; if it can
be recomputed, it is not raw. This is what makes it safe to re-run an analysis
from scratch a year later.
:::

### Raw codes and volts {#sec-volts}

When a file carries `raw`, volts are recovered with the driver's own
conversion — `Device::to_volts()`:

$$
V = \mathrm{raw} \times \frac{V_\mathrm{ref}}{2^{n_\mathrm{bits}} - 1}
$$ {#eq-to-volts}

with $V_\mathrm{ref}$ from `board.vref_mV` and $n_\mathrm{bits}$ from
`board.adc_bits`. Note the denominator: full scale is $2^n - 1$, not $2^n$.
`labtools` uses @eq-to-volts and nothing else, so a value computed on the host
after the fact equals the one `arduino-io --volts` would have written.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `adc_bits` is what the board *reports*, not always what it *delivers*

A Nano 33 BLE and a Nano RP2040 Connect report 16 bits and deliver 12
significant ones. @eq-to-volts is still the right conversion — it is the one
the driver applies — but the quantization step you should put in an
uncertainty budget is the *effective* one. S1 measures it instead of trusting
the datasheet, which is the whole point of that experiment.
:::

**Prefer `raw` in reference files.** It is the integer the ADC produced;
volts are a derived quantity that depends on `vref_mV`, and keeping the code
lets a later correction to the reference voltage be applied without
re-acquiring. All the reference data shipped with these experiments stores
`raw`.

## The YAML sidecar {#sec-sidecar}

```{.yaml filename="reference.yaml"}
experiment: S1
run: reference
date: 2026-09-18
operator: "synthetic generator"
synthetic: true

board:
  model: portenta-h7
  serial: "SYNTHETIC-0001"
  usbio_version: "0.4.0"
  adc_bits: 16
  vref_mV: 3300

host:
  os: linux
  os_version: "6.6"
  machine: "raspberry-pi-5"
  libusb_version: "1.0.27"
  hub: true

driver_version: "0.4.0"
binding: python
binding_version: "0.4.0"

acquisition:
  pins: [15, 16]
  requested_period_us: 1000
  achieved_rate_hz: 999.8
  duration_s: 10.0

stream_stats:
  records: 9998
  device_overruns: 0
  seq_gaps: 0
  host_drops: 0
  resyncs: 0
  stale_records: 0

channels:
  - pin: 15
    quantity: voltage
    unit: V
    sensor: "voltage reference IC"
    conditioning:
      gain: 1.0
      offset: 0.0
      filter: none
    calibration_reference: "DMM, see references"
  - pin: 16
    quantity: voltage
    unit: V
    sensor: "shorted input"
    conditioning:
      gain: 1.0
      offset: 0.0
      filter: none

environment:
  ambient_temperature_C: 23.0
  notes: "generated, not measured"

references:
  - instrument: DMM
    model: "TODO (Paolo)"
    calibration: "TODO (Paolo)"
```

### Field reference {#sec-fields}

Required fields are the ones without which an analysis template cannot
produce a defensible number. `labtools`' `validate_meta()` checks exactly
this list and returns a problem for each one missing.

: Sidecar fields {#tbl-sidecar}

| Field | Required | Type | Meaning |
|---|:--:|---|---|
| `experiment` | ● | string | Experiment id, e.g. `S1` |
| `run` | ● | string | Run id, unique within the experiment |
| `date` | ● | date | Acquisition date, `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `operator` | | string | Who ran it |
| `synthetic` | ● | bool | `true` for generated data. Never omit it |
| `board.model` | ● | string | Board slug, e.g. `portenta-h7` |
| `board.serial` | | string | USB serial number, as `arduino-io list` shows it |
| `board.usbio_version` | | string | Firmware version on the board |
| `board.adc_bits` | ● | int | As reported by `arduino-io info` |
| `board.vref_mV` | ● | int | As reported by `arduino-io info` |
| `host.os` | | string | `linux`, `macos`, `windows` |
| `host.os_version` | | string | |
| `host.machine` | | string | Free text; useful when comparing hosts |
| `host.libusb_version` | | string | |
| `host.hub` | | bool | Was a USB hub in the path |
| `driver_version` | | string | ArduinoDriver version |
| `binding` | | string | `python`, `r` or `cli` |
| `binding_version` | | string | |
| `acquisition.pins` | ● | list of int | Pins in the file, ascending |
| `acquisition.requested_period_us` | | int | `0` for free running |
| `acquisition.achieved_rate_hz` | | float | Per channel, from the stream summary |
| `acquisition.duration_s` | | float | |
| `stream_stats.records` | | int | From the stream summary |
| `stream_stats.device_overruns` | | int | |
| `stream_stats.seq_gaps` | | int | |
| `stream_stats.host_drops` | | int | |
| `stream_stats.resyncs` | | int | |
| `stream_stats.stale_records` | | int | |
| `channels[].pin` | ● | int | |
| `channels[].quantity` | ● | string | `voltage`, `temperature`, `strain`, … |
| `channels[].unit` | ● | string | SI unit symbol |
| `channels[].sensor` | | string | |
| `channels[].conditioning.gain` | | float | Volts per volt at the ADC input |
| `channels[].conditioning.offset` | | float | Volts added ahead of the ADC |
| `channels[].conditioning.filter` | | string | `none`, or e.g. `RC 1st order, fc = 100 Hz` |
| `channels[].calibration_reference` | | string | Which instrument set or read the reference |
| `channels[].reference_value` | | float | The applied or measured reference value, in `unit` — a calibration point |
| `channels[].reference_u` | | float | Standard uncertainty of `reference_value`, same unit |
| `environment.ambient_temperature_C` | | float | |
| `environment.notes` | | string | |
| `references[].instrument` | | string | `DMM`, `generator`, `thermometer`, … |
| `references[].model` | | string | |
| `references[].calibration` | | string | Certificate, date, or `none` |
| `generator` | | mapping | Present only in generated files: which tool and version wrote them |

::: {.callout-note}
## `stream_stats` is a data-quality record, not decoration

The stream summary line is the only evidence that a recording is complete.
Copy it into the sidecar and an analysis can refuse to draw conclusions from a
run with `seq_gaps > 0` — which is a lost sample, not a late one, and puts a
hole in the timestamp grid that a naive periodogram will happily turn into a
spectral artifact. A run with every counter at zero is a complete recording.
:::

### Filling the sidecar at the bench {#sec-checklist}

Every handbook repeats this checklist at the point where the data is taken.
The fields nobody remembers an hour later are the ones in bold.

1. **Board**: `arduino-io info` gives `adc_bits`, `vref_mV`, the firmware
   version and the board model in one go. Paste it.
2. **Host**: `uname -a` (Linux, macOS) or `systeminfo` (Windows); note whether
   a **USB hub** is in the path.
3. **Acquisition**: the requested period, and the **achieved** rate from the
   stream summary — they are not the same number.
4. **`stream_stats`**: all six counters from the summary line.
5. **Channels**: which pin measured what, through which conditioning, with
   which **gain and offset actually fitted to the board**, not the nominal
   design values.
6. **References**: the model and calibration state of every instrument whose
   reading enters the result — the DMM, the generator, the thermometer.
7. **`synthetic: false`.** For real data, say so explicitly.

## Reading a run {#sec-labtools}

Both implementations of `labtools` — Python in `shared/python/labtools`, R in
`shared/R/labtools.R` — expose the same functions with the same names and the
same numerical definitions. Every analysis template starts the same way in
either language.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

```python
from labtools import read_run, synthetic_banner, timing_summary, budget_table

run = read_run("data/reference.csv")   # .csv, .yaml or the bare stem
run.data      # pandas DataFrame: t_us, pin, raw, volts
run.meta      # dict, straight from the sidecar
```

## R

```r
source("../../shared/R/labtools.R")

run <- read_run("data/reference.csv")  # .csv, .yaml or the bare stem
run$data      # data.frame: t_us, pin, raw, volts
run$meta      # list, straight from the sidecar
```

:::

`read_run()` accepts the CSV path, the YAML path, or the shared stem, and
always returns both halves. If the CSV carries `raw` and the sidecar has
`board.adc_bits` and `board.vref_mV`, a `volts` column is added with
@eq-to-volts; if it carries `volts`, `raw` is *not* invented.

### The functions {#sec-functions}

: `labtools` in both languages {#tbl-labtools}

| Function | Returns | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `read_run(path)` | data + metadata | Reads a CSV/YAML pair; adds `volts` from `raw` when it can |
| `write_run(path, data, meta)` | — | Writes the pair back, sidecar keys in canonical order |
| `validate_meta(meta)` | list of problems | Empty list means the sidecar has every required field |
| `synthetic_banner(meta)` | markdown string | A warning callout when `synthetic: true`, empty otherwise |
| `pivot_channels(data, value)` | wide table | One column per pin, one row per timestamp |
| `timing_summary(data)` | statistics + residuals | Interval statistics and the least-squares grid fit of @sec-timing |
| `lsb_volts(meta)` | float | $V_\mathrm{ref} / (2^{n} - 1)$ |
| `u_quantization(step)` | float | $step/\sqrt{12}$ |
| `enob(fsr, sigma_r)` | float | $\log_2\left(\mathrm{FSR} / (\sqrt{12}\,\sigma_r)\right)$ |
| `budget_table(components)` | budget | The GUM uncertainty budget of @sec-budget |

Every analysis template calls `synthetic_banner()` before its first figure, in
a cell that emits raw markdown:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

````markdown
```{{python}}
#| output: asis
print(synthetic_banner(run.meta))
```
````

## R

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| output: asis
cat(synthetic_banner(run$meta))
```
````

:::

so that a reader can never mistake generated data for a measurement.

### Timing statistics {#sec-timing}

`timing_summary()` answers one question: *is the sampling grid regular, and if
not, how does it fail?* Bounded jitter and accumulating error are different
defects with different consequences, and the residuals of a grid fit separate
them cleanly.

Take the distinct timestamps $t_0 \le t_1 \le \dots \le t_{n-1}$ of the run
and fit, by ordinary least squares on the index $i$,

$$
\hat{t}_i = \hat{t}_0 + i\,\hat{T}
$$ {#eq-grid-fit}

The residuals

$$
r_i = t_i - \left(\hat{t}_0 + i\,\hat{T}\right)
$$ {#eq-grid-residual}

are the diagnostic. Residuals that scatter within a band of a few microseconds
and show no trend mean bounded jitter: the grid is right, individual samples
arrive early or late. Residuals that walk away linearly mean $\hat{T}$ is not
the true period — a clock error. Residuals with sudden steps mean the schedule
restarted, which is what the firmware does after a late record: it starts
counting again from that moment instead of emitting a burst of catch-up
records, so a hiccup shows up as one long interval and a step in $r_i$, never
as a pile-up.

The returned statistics are, in both languages:

: `timing_summary()` output {#tbl-timing}

| Name | Definition |
|---|---|
| `n` | Number of distinct timestamps |
| `duration_s` | $(t_{n-1} - t_0) \times 10^{-6}$ |
| `mean_interval_us` | Mean of $d_i = t_{i+1} - t_i$ |
| `sd_interval_us` | Sample standard deviation of $d_i$, divisor $n-2$ |
| `min_interval_us`, `max_interval_us`, `median_interval_us` | Of $d_i$ |
| `achieved_rate_hz` | $(n-1)/\texttt{duration\_s}$ |
| `period_us` | $\hat{T}$ from @eq-grid-fit |
| `t0_us` | $\hat{t}_0$ from @eq-grid-fit |
| `residual_rms_us` | $\sqrt{\overline{r_i^2}}$ |
| `residual_max_abs_us` | $\max_i \lvert r_i \rvert$ |
| `n_long_intervals` | Count of $d_i > 1.5 \times \operatorname{median}(d)$ — schedule restarts |

together with the vectors $d_i$ and $r_i$ themselves, for plotting.

::: {.callout-note}
## Timestamp quantization

`t_us` is an integer microsecond count, so every timestamp carries a
quantization uncertainty

$$
u_q = \frac{1\,\mu\mathrm{s}}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 0.29\,\mu\mathrm{s}
$$ {#eq-uq}

which is the floor below which none of these statistics means anything. At
1 kHz it is $2.9 \times 10^{-4}$ of the period and safely ignorable; at 30 kHz
it is about 1 % of it and is not.
:::

### Uncertainty budgets {#sec-budget}

`budget_table()` turns a list of uncertainty components into the table every
experiment ends with. Each component is a mapping:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

```python
budget = budget_table([
    dict(quantity="Reference voltage", value=2.5000, unit="V",
         distribution="normal", half_width=0.0004, coverage=2, sensitivity=1.0),
    dict(quantity="Quantization", value=0.0, unit="V",
         distribution="rectangular", half_width=lsb / 2, sensitivity=1.0),
    dict(quantity="Repeatability", value=0.0, unit="V",
         distribution="type-a", std=sigma / np.sqrt(n), sensitivity=1.0),
], k=2)

budget.table    # DataFrame, one row per component
budget.u_c      # combined standard uncertainty
budget.U        # expanded uncertainty, k = 2
```

## R

```r
budget <- budget_table(list(
  list(quantity = "Reference voltage", value = 2.5000, unit = "V",
       distribution = "normal", half_width = 0.0004, coverage = 2, sensitivity = 1.0),
  list(quantity = "Quantization", value = 0.0, unit = "V",
       distribution = "rectangular", half_width = lsb / 2, sensitivity = 1.0),
  list(quantity = "Repeatability", value = 0.0, unit = "V",
       distribution = "type-a", std = sigma / sqrt(n), sensitivity = 1.0)
), k = 2)

budget$table    # data.frame, one row per component
budget$u_c      # combined standard uncertainty
budget$U        # expanded uncertainty, k = 2
```

:::

The standard uncertainty of each component follows @tbl-divisors, which is the
GUM's treatment of Type B evaluations [@gum2008]:

: Distribution to standard uncertainty {#tbl-divisors}

| `distribution` | From | $u(x_i)$ |
|---|---|---|
| `normal` | `half_width` $a$, `coverage` $k_i$ (default 2) | $a/k_i$ |
| `rectangular` | `half_width` $a$ | $a/\sqrt{3}$ |
| `triangular` | `half_width` $a$ | $a/\sqrt{6}$ |
| `u-shaped` | `half_width` $a$ | $a/\sqrt{2}$ |
| `type-a` | `std` $s$ | $s$ |

Combination is the GUM's law of propagation without correlation terms:

$$
u_c = \sqrt{\sum_i \left(c_i\, u(x_i)\right)^2},
\qquad U = k\,u_c
$$ {#eq-uc}

with $c_i$ the sensitivity coefficient of each input quantity and $k = 2$ by
default, for a coverage probability of about 95 % when the combined
distribution is approximately normal. The table also reports each component's
*index* $h_i$, the fraction of the combined variance it accounts for:

$$
h_i = \frac{\left(c_i\,u(x_i)\right)^2}{u_c^2}
$$ {#eq-index}

which is the column to read when deciding what to improve. A budget where one
component holds 95 % of the variance is a budget with one thing worth fixing.

::: {.callout-warning}
## What `budget_table()` does not do

It assumes the input quantities are uncorrelated and the model is linear in
them at the operating point. Both assumptions are stated in every handbook
that uses it, and both are wrong in at least one experiment on this site —
T1's Steinhart–Hart fit is strongly nonlinear, and its handbook says what to
do instead (propagate through the fitted model, or use a Monte Carlo
evaluation as in JCGM 101 [@gum_s1]).
:::

## Processed files and figures

A template that writes anything back does so next to the raw file with a
different stem and its own sidecar, with `synthetic` copied from the source
and a `derived_from` key naming the run it came from. Nothing in AMLab
overwrites a raw file, ever.
